North Lincolnshire's population increased by around 2,200 between the last two censuses (held in 2011 and 2021). This semi-automated article highlights some of the most notable changes among the local population.

The population reached nearly 170,000

Between the last two censuses (held in 2011 and 2021), the population of North Lincolnshire increased by 1.3%, from around 167,400 in 2011 to around 169,700 in 2021.

The population here increased by a smaller percentage than the overall population of Yorkshire and The Humber (3.7%), and by a smaller percentage than the overall population of England (up 6.6% since the 2011 Census).

In 2021, North Lincolnshire was home to around 1.4 people per football pitch-sized piece of land. This area was among the lowest 25% for population density across English local authority areas at the last census.

This article generally uses percentages to enable comparisons over time and between areas. The percentage point change is also used to show the difference between the 2011 and 2021 percentages.

Population growth was lower in North Lincolnshire than across Yorkshire and The Humber

An older North Lincolnshire

Between the last two censuses, the average (median) age of North Lincolnshire increased by two years, from 42 to 44 years of age.

This area had a higher average (median) age than Yorkshire and The Humber as a whole in 2021 (40 years) and a higher average (median) age than England (40 years).

The median age is the age of the person in the middle of the group, meaning that one half of the group is younger than that person and the other half is older.

The number of people aged 65 to 74 years rose by around 4,000 (an increase of 24.5%), while the number of residents between 35 and 49 years fell by around 5,500 (15.4% decrease).

The share of residents aged between 65 and 74 years increased by 2.2 percentage points between 2011 and 2021

Health in North Lincolnshire

In 2021, 43.9% of North Lincolnshire residents described their health as "very good", increasing from 42.9% in 2011. Those describing their health as "good" fell from 36.0% to 35.9%. These are age-standardised proportions.

Age-standardised proportions are used throughout this section. They enable comparisons between populations over time and across geographies, as they account for differences in the population size and age structure.

The proportion of North Lincolnshire residents describing their health as "very bad" was 1.2% (similar to 2011), while those describing their health as "bad" fell from 4.7% to 4.5%.

These data reflect people’s own opinions in describing their overall health on a five point scale, from very good to very bad.

Census 2021 was conducted during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic. This may have influenced how people perceived and rated their health, and therefore may have affected how people chose to respond.

The percentage of people in very good health in North Lincolnshire increased by 1.0 percentage points

Change in unpaid care

North Lincolnshire saw Yorkshire and The Humber's joint third-largest percentage-point rise (alongside Barnsley and Calderdale) in the proportion of people (aged five years and over) providing between 20 and 49 hours of weekly unpaid care (from 1.5% in 2011 to 2.1% in 2021). These are age-standardised proportions.

Age-standardised proportions are used throughout this section. They enable comparisons between populations over time and across geographies, as they account for differences in the population size and age structure.

Across the region, only North East Lincolnshire (from 1.4% to 2.2%) and Bradford (from 1.7% to 2.4%) saw a greater increase in the proportion of people (aged five years and over) providing between 20 and 49 hours of weekly unpaid care.

Every local authority area across Yorkshire and The Humber saw a rise in the proportion of people (aged five years and over) providing between 20 and 49 hours of weekly unpaid care, as the regional proportion grew from 1.6% to 2.0%.

Census 2021 was undertaken during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic. This may have influenced how people perceived and managed their provision of unpaid care, and therefore may have affected how people chose to respond.

Caution should be taken when making comparisons between 2011 and 2021 because of changes in question wording and response options.

The percentage of those providing between 20 and 49 hours of weekly unpaid care in North Lincolnshire increased by 0.6 percentage points

National identity in North Lincolnshire

In 2021, 6.5% of North Lincolnshire residents did not identify with any national identity associated with the UK. This figure increased from 4.3% in 2011.

The increase in the percentage of people who did not identify with any national identity associated with the UK was greater in North Lincolnshire (2.2 percentage points) than across Yorkshire and The Humber (1.6 percentage points, from 5.1% to 6.7%). Across England, the percentage increased by 1.7 percentage points, from 8.2% to 10.0%.

In Census 2021, “British” was moved to the top response option and this may have influenced how people described their national identity. For further information, please see our quality report.

The percentage of people who did not identify with at least one UK national identity in North Lincolnshire increased by 2.2 percentage points

Rise in private renting

Of North Lincolnshire households, 17.2% rented privately in 2021, up from 13.4% in 2011.

In 2021, just over one in seven households (15.0%) lived in socially rented housing, compared with 15.4% in 2011. The percentage of North Lincolnshire households that owned their home (outright or with a mortgage or loan) decreased from 69.5% to 67.5%.

The increase in the percentage of privately-rented homes in North Lincolnshire (3.8 percentage points) was similar to the increase across Yorkshire and The Humber (3.5 percentage points, from 15.9% to 19.4%). Across England, the percentage increased by 3.6 percentage points, from 16.8% to 20.5%.

Private renting in North Lincolnshire increased by 3.8 percentage points

Religion in North Lincolnshire

In 2021, 38.6% of North Lincolnshire residents reported having "No religion", up from 24.0% in 2011. The rise of 14.7 percentage points was the largest increase of all broad religious groups in North Lincolnshire. Because the census question about religious affiliation is voluntary and has varying response rates, caution is needed when comparing figures between different areas or between censuses.

Across Yorkshire and The Humber, the percentage of residents who described themselves as having "No religion" increased from 25.9% to 39.4%, while across England the percentage increased from 24.8% to 36.7%.

In 2021, 52.1% of people in North Lincolnshire described themselves as Christian (down from 66.0%), while 5.5% did not state their religion (down from 7.1% the decade before).

There are many factors that can cause changes to the religious profile of an area, such as a changing age structure or residents relocating for work or education. Changes may also be caused by differences in the way individuals chose to self-identify between censuses. Religious affiliation is the religion with which someone connects or identifies, rather than their beliefs or religious practice.

In 2021, 38.6% of usual residents in North Lincolnshire reported having "No religion"

North Lincolnshire residents' country of birth

In the latest census, around 149,900 North Lincolnshire residents said they were born in England. This represented 88.3% of the local population. The figure has decreased from around 152,000 in 2011, which at the time represented 90.8% of North Lincolnshire's population.

Poland was the next most represented, with around 3,600 North Lincolnshire residents reporting this country of birth (2.1%). This figure was up from just over 2,600 in 2011, which at the time represented 1.6% of the population of North Lincolnshire.

The number of North Lincolnshire residents born in Scotland fell from around 2,800 in 2011 (1.7% of the local population) to just under 2,400 in 2021 (1.4%).

In 2021, 88.3% of North Lincolnshire residents reported their country of birth as England

Fewer couples without children

Of North Lincolnshire households, 19.4% included a couple but no children in 2021, down from 20.7% in 2011.

In 2021, just over one in six households (17.8%) included a couple with dependent children, compared with 19.8% in 2011. The percentage of single family households including a couple living with only non-dependent children decreased from 6.7% to 6.6%.

The decrease in the percentage of households including a couple but no children in North Lincolnshire (1.2 percentage points) was similar to the decrease across Yorkshire and The Humber (1.0 percentage points, from 18.7% to 17.7%). Across England, the percentage fell by 0.9 percentage points, from 17.6% to 16.8%.

The percentage of households including a couple without children in North Lincolnshire decreased by 1.2 percentage points

More adults never married or in a civil partnership

Of North Lincolnshire residents aged 16 years and over, 32.5% said they had never been married or in a civil partnership in 2021, up from 28.9% in 2011.

In 2021, just under one in two people (47.3%) said they were married or in a registered civil partnership, compared with 50.4% in 2011. The percentage of adults in North Lincolnshire that had divorced or dissolved a civil partnership increased from 10.5% to 10.6%.

The increase in the percentage of people aged 16 years and over who had never been married or in a civil partnership in North Lincolnshire (3.5 percentage points) was similar to the increase across Yorkshire and The Humber (3.8 percentage points, from 33.9% to 37.7%). Across England, the percentage increased by 3.3 percentage points, from 34.6% to 37.9%.

These figures include same-sex marriages and opposite-sex civil partnerships in 2021, neither of which were legally recognised in England and Wales in 2011. Same-sex marriages have been legally recognised in England and Wales since 2014 and opposite-sex civil partnerships have been recognised since 2019.

The percentage of adults who had never married or registered a civil partnership in North Lincolnshire increased by 3.5 percentage points

Fall in employment

Of North Lincolnshire residents aged 16 years and over, 53.3% said they were employed (excluding full-time students) in 2021, down from 56.0% in 2011.

The decrease in the percentage of people aged 16 years and over (excluding full-time students) who were employed was greater in North Lincolnshire (2.7 percentage points) than across Yorkshire and The Humber (1.1 percentage points, from 54.5% to 53.5%). Across England, the percentage fell by 0.8 percentage points, from 56.5% to 55.7%.

Census 2021 took place during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic, a period of rapid and unparalleled change; the national lockdown, associated guidance and furlough measures will have affected the labour market and our ability to measure it.

The percentage of people aged 16 years and over who were employed (excluding full-time students) in North Lincolnshire decreased by 2.7 percentage points

Working hours in North Lincolnshire

In 2021, 9.3% of North Lincolnshire residents aged 16 years and over and in employment said they worked 15 hours or less per week. This figure was at a similar level in 2011 (9.2%).

In 2021, just over one in nine people (11.5%) said they worked over 49 hours per week, compared with 13.2% in 2011. The percentage of adults in employment working 31 to 48 hours per week increased from 57.2% to 59.4%.

The percentage of people aged 16 years and over and in employment who said they usually worked 15 hours or less per week was 9.7% (similar to 2011) across Yorkshire and The Humber. Across England, the percentage increased from 9.7% to 10.3%.

Working hours may have been affected by the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic.

The percentage of adults who worked 15 hours or less in North Lincolnshire increased by 0.1 percentage points

Disability in North Lincolnshire

In 2021, 8.2% of North Lincolnshire residents were identified as being disabled and limited a lot. This figure decreased from 9.5% in 2011. These are age-standardised proportions.

Age-standardised proportions are used throughout this section. They enable comparisons between populations over time and across geographies, as they account for differences in the population size and age structure.

In 2021, just under one in nine people (10.8%) were identified as being disabled and limited a little, compared with 10.4% in 2011. The proportion of North Lincolnshire residents who were not disabled increased from 80.1% to 81.0%.

The decrease in the proportion of residents who were identified as being disabled and limited a lot was greater across Yorkshire and The Humber (1.7 percentage points, from 9.9% to 8.2%) than in North Lincolnshire (1.3 percentage points). Across England, the proportion fell by 1.6 percentage points, from 9.1% to 7.5%.

Census 2021 was undertaken during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic. This may have influenced how people perceived their health status and activity limitations, and therefore may have affected how people chose to respond.

Caution should be taken when making comparisons between 2011 and 2021 because of changes in question wording and response options.

The percentage of people who were identified as being disabled and limited a lot in North Lincolnshire decreased by 1.3 percentage points

Ethnic groups in North Lincolnshire

In 2021, 3.3% of North Lincolnshire residents identified their ethnic group within the "Asian, Asian British or Asian Welsh" category, up from 2.7% in 2011. The 0.6 percentage-point change was the largest increase among high-level ethnic groups in this area.

Across Yorkshire and The Humber, the percentage of people from the "Asian, Asian British or Asian Welsh" ethnic group increased from 7.3% to 8.9%, while across England the percentage increased from 7.8% to 9.6%.

In 2021, 94.3% of people in North Lincolnshire identified their ethnic group within the "White" category (compared with 96.0% in 2011), while 1.1% identified their ethnic group within the "Mixed or Multiple" category (compared with 0.7% the previous decade).

The percentage of people who identified their ethnic group within the "Other" category ("Arab" or "Any other ethnic group") increased from 0.2% in 2011 to 0.8% in 2021.

There are many factors that may be contributing to the changing ethnic composition of England and Wales, such as differing patterns of ageing, fertility, mortality, and migration. Changes may also be caused by differences in the way individuals chose to self-identify between censuses.
